{"id": "20:51/q03", "question": "What does qurūn mean?", "turns_on": "Whether shared time alone defines a qarn or an exemplary religious figure is required.", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q03/p1", "position": "Generations: people living together in one era.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says qarn is singular and explains the name by people being joined in an era; Jishumī likewise derives it from joining. Bursevī defines it as people living at the same time."}, {"id": "20:51/q03/p2", "position": "A qarn is an era with a prophet or exemplary learned leader, excluding an age of ignorant prophetic hiatus.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes this to al-Zajjāj and excludes an age of widespread ignorance without a prophet. Al-Ṭabrisī likewise reports al-Zajjāj's criterion of a prophet, imam, or scholar to emulate."}]}
{"id": "20:51/q04", "question": "Which generations are meant by 'the former'?", "turns_on": "How broadly the earlier peoples are delimited and whether Pharaoh includes himself with them.", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q04/p1", "position": "Past peoples such as Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamūd.", "reasons": "Maqātil's believer and al-Thaʿlabī cite the warning about these peoples in 40:30–31. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī identify them as idol worshippers; al-Ṭabrisī calls them nations that rejected Moses' message and worshipped idols; Bursevī asks about the detailed events that befell them."}, {"id": "20:51/q04/p2", "position": "Generations before Pharaoh, though he does not separate himself from them.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says these earliest generations end with Pharaoh's own destruction in the Qur'anic usage of al-Qaṣaṣ."}]}
{"id": "20:51/q05", "question": "How does al-ūlā agree with qurūn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q05/p1", "position": "A feminine singular adjective can describe a plural noun; al-ūlā is the feminine of al-awwal.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān compares al-qurūn al-ūlā to al-samāwāt al-ʿulā and al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā. Bursevī compares the singular pattern al-kubrā beside al-akbar."}]}
{"id": "20:51/q06", "question": "Who speaks the question?", "turns_on": "The identity of the subject of qāla.", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q06/p1", "position": "Pharaoh asks it.", "reasons": "This is explicit in Maqātil, Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, Jishumī, al-Baghawī, and the subsequent explanations of his motive and Moses' reply."}, {"id": "20:51/q06/p2", "position": "Moses asks Pharaoh about the earlier generations.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj states this assignment of the speaker."}]}
{"id": "20:51/q07", "question": "What does the speaker ask about the earlier generations?", "turns_on": "Whether the question seeks historical information, posthumous fate and recompense, the earlier peoples' worship, their earthly punishment, or God's knowledge of them.", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q07/p1", "position": "Their general condition or fate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Wāḥidī, asks after the passed generations' condition; Qatāda is reported similarly by al-Durr. Al-Wāḥidī says their deeds are preserved for recompense. Al-Baghawī names Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamūd, who worshipped idols and denied resurrection. Al-Qurṭubī places their condition among the unseen matters. Al-Nasafī speaks of past and vanished generations; Bursevī asks what detailed events befell them; the Study Quran asks what God did with them."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p2", "position": "Why earlier idol worshippers did not recognize or worship the true God, if Moses' proof is clear.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī frames this as whether they shared Moses' faith. Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, and Abū Ḥayyān mention idol worship. Al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān explain the appeal to inherited belief against a supposedly obvious proof of the Creator; Elmalılı says the question seeks to deny guidance and prophecy. Ibn Kathīr explicitly prefers this reading."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p3", "position": "Why dead generations have not been raised, judged, and repaid.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and al-Māwardī tie this to Moses' call to believe in resurrection; Jishumī cites the warning of punishment in 20:48 and, in another formulation, a threat of hell after long discussion. Al-Ṭabrisī reports the same link. Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān explicitly include judgment and recompense. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says death seems to leave only reports and legends, and compares the objection to 32:10 on recreation after becoming dust."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p4", "position": "What becomes of them after death: who is blessed and who is wretched.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says the happy and wretched are unseen to Moses. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī frame the question as their posthumous states; the Study Quran asks what God did with them. Al-Qāshānī reads this as the self's concealment from resurrection and afterlife happiness and misery."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p5", "position": "The deeds of earlier generations.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives this paraphrase in Yaḥyā ibn Sallām; al-Wāḥidī says Pharaoh asks after Moses' preceding answer."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p6", "position": "Their sins and the punishment they received, or why earlier deniers were not punished.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī asks about their sins and punishment. Al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān relate the challenge to Moses' warning that deniers are punished. Kur'an Yolu takes it as a question whether the powerful can escape consequences; Moses answers that they remain recorded with God."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p7", "position": "The histories and circumstances of vanished peoples.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī attributes this to Maqātil; Abū Ḥayyān says Pharaoh may be testing whether Moses and Aaron are prophets or storytellers, before the Torah's revelation. Bursevī names the past events of Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamūd. Iṣlāḥī calls the question sarcastic: a messenger ought to know those histories. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ reports this from many commentators but objects to the interpretation as a distraction."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p8", "position": "What blinded those earlier generations.", "reasons": "Qatāda adds that their lifespans and appointed terms are with God, referring to 20:52 and 7:187."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p9", "position": "Whether past polytheists were irretrievably doomed.", "reasons": "Asad supplies this as Pharaoh's implied challenge about generations who worshipped multiple gods."}, {"id": "20:51/q07/p10", "position": "How God knows every distant generation and all its parts.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes this possibility to al-Zamakhsharī: Moses replies that every being is known and recorded, unlike Pharaoh's fallible knowledge."}]}
{"id": "20:51/q08", "question": "Why does Pharaoh raise this question now?", "turns_on": "Which prior claim prompts Pharaoh and whether he seeks a substantive challenge, a prophetic test, or a diversion; Bursevī contests who voiced the earlier warning, while al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ contests the diversion reading.", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q08/p1", "position": "He diverts Moses from a compelling proof to confuse the audience and avoid answering.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya call it evasion; Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī compare the tactic to innovators or heretics changing subjects when proof appears. Al-Rāzī prefers this: Pharaoh feared his falsehood would be exposed, and Moses returned to the proof of divine oneness. Abū Ḥayyān calls it sophistry after Moses silenced him; al-Biqāʿī calls the new dispute broad and unprovable. Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Iṣlāḥī, and Kur'an Yolu stress protecting Pharaoh's influence or making Moses seem uninformed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ reports the history-diversion reading from many commentators but rejects it as strange because the questions connect to the preceding argument."}, {"id": "20:51/q08/p2", "position": "He challenges Moses' proof through the ancestral failure to recognize God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls it an appeal to inherited belief; Abū Ḥayyān says Pharaoh asks why past peoples missed an allegedly obvious rational proof. Elmalılı says he seeks to deny divine guidance and prophethood. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a direct contradiction reading but finds it ill fitted: generations before Moses' claim could not have rejected that claim."}, {"id": "20:51/q08/p3", "position": "He challenges the promise of resurrection and punishment for deniers.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, Jishumī, and al-Ṭabrisī connect the move to Moses' call for resurrection and warning of punishment. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says 20:48 warned of punishment, idolaters reject it, and the apparent disappearance of the dead makes recompense seem incredible; the parallel is 32:10. He adds that guidance through prophecy and resurrection is needed for judgment to distinguish good from evil and make God's commands and approval known."}, {"id": "20:51/q08/p4", "position": "He asks after hearing a warning about the fate of earlier nations.", "reasons": "Maqātil assigns the warning about Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd and later peoples to the believer from Pharaoh's household, citing 40:30–31. Al-Thaʿlabī says it followed Moses' warning. Al-Naqqāsh, reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān, connects it to that believer. Bursevī reports al-Asʾila al-Muqḥima's view that Moses voiced the warning, then rejects that attribution: the fa fits, but the reply does not, and the speaker was the believer, whom the context does not identify with Moses."}, {"id": "20:51/q08/p5", "position": "He tests whether Moses, claiming to be a messenger, can recount what happened long before him.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says fa connects the question to the messenger claim. Iṣlāḥī calls Pharaoh's request sarcastic; Abū Ḥayyān says it tests whether Moses and Aaron are prophets or storytellers."}]}

s": [{"id": "20:51/q09/p1", "position": "Their histories were not yet revealed to him, because the Torah came after Pharaoh's destruction.", "reasons": "Maqātil says Moses could not tell their fate for this chronological reason; al-Naqqāsh is reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān, and Ibn al-Jawzī attributes a similar account to Maqātil. Abū Ḥayyān also connects it with Pharaoh's test of Moses before the Torah."}, {"id": "20:51/q09/p2", "position": "Their unseen fate and histories belong to God's knowledge; a messenger knows only what God reveals.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports another view that a messenger does not know unseen reports; al-Rāzī contrasts Moses' rational answer to a question about God with his referral of transmitted history to the Knower of the unseen. Al-Qurṭubī states the limit of revelation, and al-Kashshāf locates happiness and wretchedness in the unseen. Al-Wāḥidī says deeds are preserved for recompense; Kur'an Yolu says God neither errs nor forgets. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ links Moses' reply to the apparent erasure of the dead and their deeds."}, {"id": "20:51/q09/p3", "position": "God's eternal, errorless knowledge encompasses and records their states, grounding knowledge of the afterlife in His attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads the question as the self's concealment from resurrection and afterlife happiness or misery; Moses' response refers to the Preserved Tablet. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's suggestion that Pharaoh tests God's encompassing knowledge of remote generations and their parts, to which Moses contrasts divine record with Pharaoh's fallibility."}]}
{"id": "20:51/q10", "question": "What other grammatical observations occur among the notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q10/p1", "position": "Demonstratives and relatives have distinctive diminutive patterns and endings.", "reasons": "Sibawayh says demonstratives retain their initial vowels and add final alifs; he gives hādhā to hadhayyā, dhāka to dhayyāka and alā to alayyā. He locates the diminutive yāʾ of dhā in third position and deletes one crowded yāʾ; tayyā is from tā. He cites Kaʿb al-Ghanawī and ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān for tamānī and hātā. Extended ulāʾ becomes ulayyāʾ, with feminine forms avoiding ambiguity. Relative alladhī and allatī yield alladhayyā and allatayyā, supported by al-ʿAjjāj; final alifs drop in duals through frequent use. Relative man and ayyu resist diminution because they remain interrogative forms, unlike alladhī; allātī needs no diminutive because allatiyyāt supplies it, compared to masiyyān and ʿashiyyān instead of a diminutive of qaṣr."}, {"id": "20:51/q10/p2", "position": "Feminine diminutives take or omit tāʾ according to word structure, established usage, and whether the name is a shared adjective.", "reasons": "Sibawayh adds tāʾ to three-letter feminine nouns; al-Khalīl says it marks femininity but ʿanāq omits it for heaviness. Shortened samāʾ gives sumayya; a woman named Siqāʾ gives siqīqī without suffix. He reports two analyses of ḥubārā, one preserving a feminine marker and another retaining a four-letter form; a late-position feminine alif yields lughayghīza from lughayzā. A shared masculine adjective such as niṣf, riḍā or khalīq remains masculine for a woman. Al-Khalīl analyzes she-camel al-nāb as nuyayyib on its established masculine name. Pure female proper names Ḥajar and Faras give Ḥujayra and Furaysa. Sibawayh omits tāʾ for a man named ʿAyn or Udhun, while Yūnus adds it and cites Udhayna."}, {"id": "20:51/q10/p3", "position": "Feminine double-alif endings are diptote, while superficially similar hamzas and reduplicated forms have other analyses.", "reasons": "Sibawayh says the second alif becomes hamza to avoid adjacent vowelless letters and retains the feminine marking effect in definite and indefinite use. The pattern does not merely lengthen triliterals; ʿalbāʾ and ḥirbāʾ instead replace yāʾ, with alif plus yāʾ lengthening. Some Arabs use masculine declinable qūbāʾ like fusṭāṭ. Ghawghāʾ can be feminine diptote like ʿawrāʾ or masculine declinable with reduplicated sounds like qaḍqāḍ or qamqām."}, {"id": "20:51/q10/p4", "position": "Weak-letter substitution and reduplication account for several long verbal and nominal forms.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl says five-letter verbs such as aghzaytu and ghāzaytu turn wāw to yāʾ after the imperfect loses wāw under kasra; taghāzaynā and tarjaynā then show alif replacing that yāʾ, with tāʾ added to ghāzaytu and rajaytu. Sibawayh treats ḍawḍaytu and qawqaytu as paired reduplication parallel to ḥayaytu and quwwa; ḥāḥaytu and ʿāʿaytu similarly substitute alif for yāʾ, supported by al-ḥayḥāʾ and al-ʿayʿāʾ. Al-Khalīl derives dahdaytu al-juʿal from dahdahtu, yāʾ replacing light hāʾ. Ghawghāʾ has feminine diptote or masculine declinable reduplicated analyses; related forms analogize to qamqām, ghaṣaṣ and ghaṣṣa. Mūmāh has root mīm like dūdāh and marmar, since an added initial mīm is rare; fīfāh has extra alif because al-fayyif has the same meaning. Qayqāʾ and zayzāʾ follow ʿalbāʾ, while qalqāl is only a verbal noun; added fourth-position yāʾ behaves like a root in salqaytu and jaʿbaytu. Al-murūrāh follows al-shujūjāh and ṣamḥamaḥ as the more common pattern, not ʿathawthal. Qayqāʾa and zayzāʾa are singulars; some say qayqāʾa and qawqāq, with substitution like qīl. Athfiyya is fiʿliyya for speakers of athaftu, but afʿūla for speakers of thafaytu."}, {"id": "20:51/q10/p5", "position": "A relative clause after ayyu-hum is regular with huwa; omission is awkward or, in a longer construction, rare.", "reasons": "Sibawayh accepts ayyu-hum huwa afḍal and similar clauses, but judges ayyu-hum ʿāqil awkward. Al-Khalīl reports an Arab's rare mā anā bi-lladhī qāʾil laka shayʾan; Sibawayh rejects a shortened version with munṭaliq, saying few use even the longer possibility."}]}

{"id": "20:51/q12", "question": "What other observations about Qur'anic interpretation occur among the notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:51/q12/p1", "position": "The community could preserve and read one of seven revealed aḥruf; the other six were neither abrogated nor forgotten.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes the Prophet's reports about seven wordings from the present written Qur'an and compares the permitted choice to selecting one of three expiations for a broken oath."}, {"id": "20:51/q12/p2", "position": "Study of rhetorical artistry is essential for explaining Qur'anic inimitability and coherence.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ criticizes earlier neglect and singles out al-Rāzī for brief treatment in al-Nihāya despite his theological command. Al-Alusi reports variants focused on failure to infer the Creator from creation or guidance, and on denial of revelation followed by punishment; the answer refers the matter to divine knowledge or decree."}, {"id": "20:52/q01/p2", "position": "He diverted Moses from a persuasive argument by raising ancestral history or fate.", "reasons": "Razi prefers fear that Moses would expose Pharaoh publicly. {"id": "20:52/q03", "question": "Why does Moses leave this knowledge with his Lord?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either Moses' limited revelation and refusal of a fruitless inquiry, or the substantive assurance of divine knowledge and judgment; both can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "20:52/q03/p1", "position": "The unseen details belong to God; Moses knows only what revelation has taught him and keeps to his mission.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says he did not know why some strayed. Al-Tha'labi, Muqatil through al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Anbari, al-Baghawi, and al-Biqa'i say the Torah telling their histories came only after Pharaoh perished. Al-Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, and Alusi distinguish a prophet's mission from unrestricted unseen knowledge. Ibn Ashur says Moses knew their general circumstances, not each person's details; he compares the Prophet's answer concerning polytheists' children. Study Quran calls the matter unfathomable."}, {"id": "20:52/q03/p2", "position": "The reply affirms that God fully knows the earlier peoples and will judge their deeds.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq says their deeds are preserved for repayment. Al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, al-Tabataba'i, and Islahi emphasize full knowledge, record, and recompense. Baydawi says the answer includes all people's parts and states. Asad says God alone can assess inner motives and errors."}]}
{"id": "20:52/q04", "question": "How are 'its knowledge,' 'with my Lord,' and 'in a book' parsed?", "turns_on": "Which phrase functions as predicate, whether a circumstance may precede an implied governor, and whether two independently predicative phrases can form one predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "20:52/q04/p1", "position": "‘With my Lord’ is the first predicate and ‘in a book’ the second, or is attached to the first predicate's implied existential verb.", "reasons": "Al-Samin also permits 'in a book' as a circumstantial modifier of the hidden subject. Al-Alusi prefers the two-predicate analysis and says a verbal noun cannot govern across its predicate."}, {"id": "20:52/q04/p2", "position": "‘In a book’ is the predicate, while ‘with my Lord’ attaches to its implied verb or serves as a circumstantial phrase or modifier.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi gives this as a principal analysis and mentions other attachments. Al-Samin allows 'with my Lord' to modify the knowledge or the genitive pronoun; al-Akhfash supports fronting the circumstance with 39:67 and poetry, and other grammarians readily front an adverbial circumstance. Al-Samin rejects making 'in a book' modify 'knowledge' once 'with my Lord' has become the predicate, because the verbal noun and its complement cannot be split."}, {"id": "20:52/q04/p3", "position": "The two prepositional phrases together form one semantic predicate.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa compares the combination to 'sweet and sour.' Al-Samin objects that each phrase can predicate independently, unlike that example."}]}
{"id": "20:52/q05", "question": "What is the book containing this knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether 'book' denotes a real heavenly or angelic record, or figures the permanence and certainty of God's knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "20:52/q05/p1", "position": "The Preserved Tablet or Preserved Record.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi, al-Kalbi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqa'i, Bursevi, and Study Quran identify it thus; Study Quran cites 85:22. Ibn Atiyya allows this alongside an angelic record. Baydawi and Alusi present it as one possibility; Alusi says the actual inscriptions stand for recorded knowledge."}, {"id": "20:52/q05/p2", "position": "A record written or kept by angels of people's deeds and circumstances.", "reasons": "Qatada speaks of deeds and lifespans. Ibn Atiyya permits the record angels wrote; al-Tabrisi reports this view, and al-Qurtubi says a book may be with one angel. Al-Biqa'i notes angels assigned to recording servants' affairs. Ibn Kathir mentions the record of deeds alongside the Preserved Tablet."}, {"id": "20:52/q05/p3", "position": "A metaphor or simile for God's firm, detailed, permanent knowledge, like an established written register.", "reasons": "Razi offers this second interpretation and argues the following denial of error and forgetfulness supports it; he objects that a literal book could suggest to Pharaoh that God needs it. Baydawi likens it to a scholar's written information. Alusi says an ordinary register used as simile may be preferable. Ibn Ashur adds the possibility that writing conveys certainty and cites al-Harith ibn Hilliza's verse."}]}
{"id": "20:52/q06", "question": "Why is knowledge said to be in a book?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish the record's benefit to angels, its honor and judgment, and its assurance of precision without divine dependence on writing.", "positions": [{"id": "20:52/q06/p1", "position": "The record displays God's knowledge and decree to angels so they can recognize its accuracy in due time.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi says angels learn at the appointed time. {"id": "20:55/q16", "question": "Does the verse include the soul in bodily resurrection?", "turns_on": "Whether the resurrected body necessarily contains the same soul.", "positions": [{"id": "20:55/q16/p1", "position": "The plural addresses body and soul together, related through death and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī answers philosophers who call spirit neither subtle body, force, nor form but governor of body, and some who deny its return to its former body; even in ʿIlliyyīn it remains tied to a body experiencing pain and pleasure.
